clueText.nc-c: Raw turbidity stayed in its usual band, which clears a raw-water spike.

tasks.prompt: Clarifier performance fell sharply during a wet-weather day even though chemical treatment looks correct.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Plant flow rose from 90 L/s to 175 L/s over three hours as storm runoff entered the source.
The surface overflow rate is now roughly double the rate the clarifier normally runs at.
Floc is well formed and settles quickly in a cylinder test, leaving clear water above.
The sludge blanket is at normal depth and sludge withdrawal is running.
Settled turbidity improves noticeably during a brief period when flow eases back toward 120 L/s.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The clarifier is hydraulically overloaded, so floc does not have enough settling time or area
The coagulant dose is too low for the raw water
The sludge blanket has built up and is washing out
The flocculator is shearing the floc before settling

inference.explanation: Flow and overflow rate doubled, floc settles well in a cylinder, the blanket is normal, and performance recovers when flow eases. That is hydraulic overload. Dose and shear are disproven by the cylinder test, and the blanket measurement clears washout.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the overload threshold for this basin?

options.label: Archived settled turbidity versus plant flow records from past wet-weather events
Archived sludge pump run log
Archived alum dose log

nextClue.explanation: Past event records show the flow above which this basin historically loses settled-water quality.

clueText.nc-a: Past events show settled turbidity climbing whenever flow passes about 140 L/s, and today the plant ran at 175 L/s for hours.
clueText.nc-b: The sludge pump ran normally, which matches the normal blanket depth.
clueText.nc-c: The dose log shows the dose was raised with flow as intended.

tasks.prompt: Sludge is accumulating in a deep cone at the centre of a circular clarifier, and settled quality is slowly worsening.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The sludge rake drive shows a high-torque alarm history and the rake arm does not move when observed.
Sludge sampled at the centre is old, dark, and releases gas bubbles when disturbed.
Blanket depth is very uneven: deep at the centre, thin near the walls.
Sludge withdrawal from the centre hopper draws mostly thin, watery sludge despite the deep centre blanket.
Influent floc quality and plant flow are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge rake has stopped, so sludge is not being moved to the withdrawal hopper
The sludge withdrawal pump has lost capacity
The coagulant dose is producing too much sludge for the basin
The clarifier is short-circuiting along one wall

inference.explanation: The rake does not move, torque alarms are logged, the blanket is deep at the centre and thin at the walls, and centre sludge is old and gassy. That is a stopped rake. A weak pump would not leave the blanket pattern uneven, dose affects both zones equally, and short-circuiting would show a flow path rather than a centre cone.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the rake stoppage?

options.label: Archived rake drive torque and run status trend
Archived sludge pump capacity test
Archived dye tracer study

nextClue.explanation: The rake drive trend shows when torque spiked and motion stopped.

clueText.nc-a: The trend shows torque spiking to the trip point six days ago, with no run time since, matching the age of the centre sludge.
clueText.nc-b: The pump capacity test was satisfactory last month, and the pump draws what reaches the hopper.
clueText.nc-c: The tracer study from commissioning showed even flow distribution, not a centre sludge cone.

tasks.prompt: One side of a rectangular clarifier produces noticeably cloudier water over its weir than the other side.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A thick mat of green algae and slime coats the effluent launder and weir plates on the cloudy side only.
Water depth over the weir plate is uneven, with visibly more flow spilling at the slime-coated sections.
The clean side of the same basin produces settled water at 1.1 NTU; the cloudy side measures 2.9 NTU.
Floc quality, dose, flow, and blanket depth are normal and even across the basin.
The launder on the cloudy side was last cleaned eight months ago; the clean side was cleaned last month.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Algae and slime growth on the weir has made flow over the weir uneven and is sloughing solids into the effluent
The basin is short-circuiting from inlet to outlet
The sludge blanket has risen on one side of the basin
The coagulant dose is too low on one side of the basin

inference.explanation: Growth is heavy on the cloudy side only, flow over that weir is uneven, the other side of the same basin is clear, and cleaning history differs by side. That points to the fouled weir. Dose is common to the whole basin, the blanket is even, and a short circuit would not follow the launder cleaning pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the weir growth effect?

options.label: Archived launder cleaning records paired with side-by-side settled turbidity samples
Archived inlet flow distribution study
Archived alum dose log

nextClue.explanation: Cleaning records against paired samples show whether turbidity follows the fouled sections.

clueText.nc-a: Past records show the same side-by-side turbidity gap whenever that launder went more than six months between cleanings, closing after each cleaning.
clueText.nc-b: The flow study showed even inlet distribution, which argues against a one-sided flow path.
clueText.nc-c: The dose log is a single common feed and cannot differ by side.

tasks.prompt: A northern Ontario clarifier loses settled-water quality every cold snap, with floc appearing at the weir soon after the basin ices over.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A continuous ice sheet covers about 70 percent of the basin surface.
Open water is confined to a channel between the inlet and the effluent launder.
Dye added at the inlet reaches the weir in about 25 minutes, against a theoretical detention time near 3 hours.
Floc settles well in an indoor cylinder test at the same dose.
Plant flow is at its normal winter rate and the blanket is at normal depth.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The ice cover has shrunk the effective basin area, channelling flow from inlet to outlet
Cold water has stopped the coagulant from working at all
The sludge blanket has frozen and is lifting into the effluent
The plant flow has risen beyond the clarifier rating

inference.explanation: Most of the surface is ice, flow is confined to a channel, dye crosses in 25 minutes, and floc settles well indoors. The ice has cut the effective settling area and created a channel. Coagulation still works per the cylinder test, flow is normal, and no blanket lifting is observed.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the ice channelling pattern?

options.label: Archived winter tracer and settled turbidity records from past cold snaps
Archived alum delivery records
Archived sludge blanket surveys

nextClue.explanation: Past cold snap tracer records show whether ice cover produced the same fast channel each winter.

clueText.nc-a: Past winters show dye crossing in under 30 minutes whenever ice cover passed about half the surface, with normal times in open water.
clueText.nc-b: Alum deliveries were on schedule, and the cylinder test already shows the chemical works.
clueText.nc-c: Blanket surveys through the winter stayed in the normal range.

tasks.prompt: The clarifier sludge blanket keeps rising even though the sludge pump runs continuously and sounds normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Sludge discharged at the pump outlet is thin and watery, with almost no solids, even with the pump running.
Suction pressure at the pump is abnormally high vacuum, and flow through the sludge line is a trickle.
Tapping along the sludge line finds a long section that sounds solid and does not vibrate with flow.
Blanket depth has risen steadily for four days and settled turbidity is beginning to suffer.
A spare pump connected to a different draw-off point pulls thick sludge normally.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge line is plugged, so the running pump cannot actually remove sludge
The sludge pump impeller is worn out
The clarifier is producing far more sludge than normal
The blanket depth gauge is reading falsely high

inference.explanation: Discharge is watery, suction vacuum is high with a trickle of flow, a line section sounds solid, and a spare pump on another draw-off pulls thick sludge. That is a plugged line. A worn impeller would not give high vacuum with a solid-sounding line, sludge production has no supporting observation, and the rising blanket is confirmed by the spare pump result.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms where this line plugs?

options.label: Archived sludge line flushing and rodding maintenance history
Archived pump curve test results
Archived raw-water solids loading records

nextClue.explanation: The line maintenance history shows the section that has plugged before and how it was cleared.

clueText.nc-a: History shows the same low elbow has plugged three times in five years, each time with high suction vacuum and watery discharge, and was cleared by rodding.
clueText.nc-b: Pump curve tests last year were within tolerance, matching the spare pump performance.
clueText.nc-c: Raw solids loading is in its normal range, so sludge production is not the change.

tasks.prompt: Of two identical clarifiers fed from a common header, Clarifier A now produces poor settled water while Clarifier B produces excellent water.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A flow check shows Clarifier A receiving about 65 percent of plant flow and Clarifier B about 35 percent.
The splitter box gate to Clarifier B is found two thirds closed, with a bent stem.
Floc quality in the common flocculation basin ahead of both clarifiers is good.
Clarifier B settled turbidity is 0.9 NTU; Clarifier A is 3.7 NTU.
Both sludge blankets are at normal depth and both rakes are turning.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The flow split is uneven, hydraulically overloading Clarifier A while Clarifier B is underloaded
Clarifier A has a coagulation problem that Clarifier B does not
Clarifier A sludge rake has failed
Clarifier A effluent turbidimeter is reading falsely high

inference.explanation: Measured flow is split 65 to 35, the gate to B is two thirds closed with a bent stem, and both clarifiers share the same flocculated water. A is simply overloaded. Coagulation is common to both, A rake is turning, and B good result beside A poor result at higher loading fits hydraulics, not a meter fault.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the flow split history?

options.label: Archived splitter box gate position and flow balance records
Archived jar test log
Archived rake drive current log

nextClue.explanation: Gate position and balance records show when the split drifted away from even.

clueText.nc-a: Records show the split was even until the gate stem was reported bent last month, after which A share crept from 50 to 65 percent.
clueText.nc-b: Jar tests were normal, matching the good floc seen in the common basin.
clueText.nc-c: Rake current on both units is normal, consistent with both rakes turning.

tasks.prompt: On warm afternoons, clumps of sludge rise to the clarifier surface and drift over the weir, while mornings are usually clear.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Rising sludge clumps carry small gas bubbles and break apart at the surface.
Sludge in the blanket is dark, has a stale odour, and blanket samples show it has been in the basin a long time.
The problem is worst after sunny, warm afternoons and absent on cool mornings.
Sludge withdrawal rates have been at the low end of the normal range for several weeks.
Influent floc is normal and plant flow is steady.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Old sludge held too long in the blanket is becoming septic and floating up on trapped gas
The coagulant dose is too high and making the floc buoyant
Wind is blowing surface water toward the effluent launder
The inlet flow is short-circuiting to the outlet in the afternoon

inference.explanation: Clumps rise on gas bubbles, the blanket sludge is dark and stale, withdrawal has run low for weeks, and the pattern follows warm afternoons. That is septic, gas-lifted sludge from excessive blanket age. Dose does not explain bubbles and odour, and wind or short-circuiting would not depend on sludge age.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms excessive sludge age?

options.label: Archived sludge withdrawal volumes and blanket age estimates for the past month
Archived wind speed records
Archived alum dose trend

nextClue.explanation: Withdrawal volumes against solids loading give the blanket age trend that leads to septicity.

clueText.nc-a: Records show withdrawal ran about 40 percent below the rate needed to match solids loading for a month, so average sludge age roughly doubled before the floating began.
clueText.nc-b: Wind records show calm afternoons on several of the worst days, which clears wind drift.
clueText.nc-c: The dose trend is flat, so a dose change does not explain the new pattern.
